author: John Chrysostom
occasion: Chrysostom preaches on the apostolic reading Romans 16:3, where Paul says, 'Greet Priscilla and Aquila.' He wants to show that even a bare greeting in Scripture is not superfluous, and to correct his hearers' neglect of Scripture, their contempt for manual labor and poverty, and, in the second homily, their slander of clergy.
argument: Chrysostom argues that no part of Scripture, even a simple greeting, is superfluous. From Paul's greeting to Priscilla and Aquila he draws lessons about true nobility, the dignity of marriage and manual labor, and the virtue of hospitality. He then defends the apostles against the charge of disobeying Christ's command to possess nothing, explaining that the command was temporary and for their training. Finally, he turns to the duty of honoring priests and warns against slandering spiritual fathers, using biblical examples to show the danger of judging others.

outline.move: Chrysostom rebukes his hearers for thinking parts of Scripture, especially greetings, are superfluous, and contrasts their zeal for horse racing and theater with their ignorance of Paul's letters.
He introduces the greeting to Priscilla and Aquila and marvels at Paul's care for two obscure tentmakers despite his worldwide ministry.
He argues that true nobility comes from virtue, not wealth or ancestry, and that Paul was not ashamed of his fellow tentmakers.
He praises Priscilla and Aquila's hospitality and virtue, noting that Paul stayed with them two years, and explains why Priscilla is named before her husband.

He discusses women's role in teaching, distinguishing public teaching from private instruction, uses Priscilla's instruction of Apollos as a positive example, and urges men and women to imitate Priscilla's zeal.
He extols hospitality and poverty, contrasting outward luxury with the inner beauty of a hospitable soul.
He praises manual labor, showing that Paul worked night and day, and rebukes those who are ashamed of working.
He illustrates how idleness corrupts everything, using water, iron, and land as examples, and exhorts his hearers to flee idleness.

He begins the second homily by recalling the benefits of the previous sermon and raises the question of why Peter had sandals and Paul had a cloak when Christ commanded the apostles to possess nothing.
He answers critics who misuse Christ's commands, and begins to explain that the command was given only to the apostles and only for a limited time.
He shows from Christ's words that the command was temporary, given to train the apostles, and later relaxed before his passion.
He explains that Christ first carried the apostles like young birds, then allowed them to struggle so their own virtue would be tested.
He interprets the command to buy a sword as a veiled prediction of the coming persecution, not a literal command to arm.
He returns to Priscilla and Aquila, praising them for risking their necks for Paul, and explains that by saving the teacher of the world, they became common benefactors of all the churches.
He argues that the poor and detached are freer and more useful to the churches than the rich, citing John the Baptist and Elijah.
He contrasts the early Christians' devotion to their teachers with his hearers' slander of their spiritual fathers, and warns of the danger of speaking against clergy.
He explains that God will judge people not only for their own sins but also for how they judged others, using the Pharisee and the tax collector as an example.
He gives further examples—David and Saul, the ark of the covenant—to show the honor due to rulers and priests, even when they are unworthy.
He concludes by urging his hearers to examine their own lives rather than slander others, so that they may escape judgment and obtain eternal goods.

scripture: Chrysostom quotes the Septuagint and the Greek New Testament. He refers to the Psalms by their LXX numbering, which is usually one behind the Hebrew numbering. In a modern translation, cite Psalms by LXX numbering with a note, or convert to Hebrew numbering with a note. He refers to the books of Kingdoms (1-4 Kingdoms = 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings). New Testament citations follow standard book names.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is not stated in the text.
The precise occasion or liturgical setting is not specified beyond the reading from Romans.
Whether the two homilies were delivered on consecutive days or at different times is not stated.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Chrysostom preaches on the apostolic reading Romans 16:3, where Paul says, 'Greet Priscilla and Aquila.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: Chrysostom preaches on the apostolic reading containing the greeting 'Greet Priscilla and Aquila' (Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν). The exact verse reference Romans 16:3 is not stated in the text; Chrysostom quotes the greeting as Ἀσπάσασθε, not Ἀσπάζεσθε (the form in Rom 16:3), though this may reflect quotation from memory or textual variation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: in the second homily, their slander of clergy
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ εἰς τὸ μὴ κακῶς λέγειν τοὺς ἱερεῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ. Λόγος βʹ.
_unresolved_facts.fix: in the second homily, their speaking evil of God's priests (κακῶς λέγειν τοὺς ἱερεῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ). The Greek specifies 'priests of God,' not 'clergy' generally; the concern is specifically about slander of priests/ἱερεῖς, though the discussion broadens to spiritual fathers and rulers.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He then defends the apostles against the charge of disobeying Christ's command to possess nothing
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων ζῶντες πόνων, ὁρῶντες πολλάκις τινὰς τῶν πιστῶν δι' ἀῤῥωστίαν σώματος πλείονα περιβεβλημένους ἱμάτια, τὸν νόμον εὐθέως ἡμῖν τοῦ Χριστοῦ προβάλλονται, καὶ ταῦτα λέγουσι τὰ ῥήματα· Οὐκ ἐκέλευσεν ὑμῖν ὁ Χριστὸς μὴ ἔχειν δύο χιτῶνας, μηδὲ ὑποδήματα; πῶς οὖν ὑμεῖς παραβαίνετε τὸν νόμον τὸν περὶ τούτων κείμενον;
_unresolved_facts.fix: He then defends the apostles (and by extension all Christians) against the charge of disobeying Christ's command to possess nothing, raised by Greek critics who mock believers. The defense is framed as a response to outsiders (τὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἐμφράξαι στόματα), not an internal church dispute.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['5'], move: 'He discusses women's role in teaching, distinguishing public teaching from private instruction, uses Priscilla's instruction of Apollos as a positive example, and urges men and women to imitate Priscilla's zeal.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ πῶς Τιμοθέῳ γράφων φησὶ, Γυναικὶ δὲ διδάσκειν οὐκ ἐπιτρέπω, οὐδὲ αὐθεντεῖν τοῦ ἀνδρός; ... ἰδίᾳ δὲ παραινεῖν καὶ συμβουλεύειν οὐκ ἐκώλυσεν. Οὐ γὰρ ἂν, εἰ κεκωλυμένον ἦν, ταύτην ἐπῄνεσε τοῦτο ποιοῦσαν. δʹ. Ἀκουέτωσαν ἄνδρες, ἀκουέτωσαν ταῦτα καὶ γυναῖκες· ἐκεῖναι μὲν, ἵνα τὴν ὁμόφυλον καὶ συγγενῆ μιμήσωνται· οὗτοι δὲ, ἵνα μὴ γυναικὸς ἀσθενέστεροι φαίνωνται.
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ['5'], move: 'He discusses women's role in teaching, distinguishing public teaching from private instruction, uses Priscilla's instruction of Apollos as a positive example, urges men and women to imitate Priscilla's zeal, and exhorts rulers and ruled, priests and laity to pursue virtue rather than wealth, and to practice hospitality.' The section also contains extensive exhortation to rulers, priests, and laity about not admiring the rich, not being ashamed of the poor, and practicing hospitality (ἄρχοντες, ἀρχόμενοι, ἱερεῖς, λαϊκοί).

_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ['9'], move: 'He begins the second homily by asking whether his hearers have learned not to consider anything in Scripture superfluous, recalls the benefits of the previous sermon (on work, idleness, Paul's soul, hospitality, poverty, virtue), and raises the question of why Peter had sandals and Paul had a cloak (φελόνην) when Christ commanded the apostles to possess nothing.'

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἵτινες ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου, φησὶ, τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον ὑπέθηκαν... οἱ τὸν διδάσκαλον τῆς οἰκουμένης διασώσαντες... κοινοὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης ἦσαν εὐεργέται, ἐν τῇ περὶ τὸν διδάσκαλον προνοίᾳ τοὺς μαθητὰς ἅπαντας διασώσαντες
